extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and legal scholars (practitioners in patent litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules governing who may be plaintiff or defendant in patent infringement suits, including standing of patentees, assignees, grantees, licensees, personal representatives, and assignees of past-claim rights, and related joinder/non-joinder principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee cannot sue in own name
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee of a patent cannot bring a suit in his own name, at law or in equity, for its infringement by a stranger. An action at law for the benefit of the licensee must be brought in the name of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities and cases (e.g., Ingalls v. Tice, Bogart v. Hinds, Wilson v. Chickering). The treatise explains that the licensee's remedy at law generally must be pursued in the patentee's name; exceptions and nuances follow in related entries (see 'Licensee may sue when patentee refuses or is inaccessible').

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee may sue if patentee refuses or is inaccessible
rubrics_metrics.description: If the legal owner of the monopoly refuses to institute proceedings to protect the licensee, or is inaccessible, the licensee may sue at law for damages in his own name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arises from an implied agreement that the licensor will protect the licensee; cases cited support a licensee's right to sue where the patentee fails to perform the duty to protect. Examples and authorities are cited in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive licensee not necessarily proper plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee having an exclusive right to sell for certain territory is not a proper plaintiff in an infringement action; only the owner of the patent (patentee) is generally the proper plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited (e.g., Ingalls v. Tice). The treatise distinguishes exclusive licenses from full assignments and treats remedies accordingly—whether an instrument is a true assignment or merely a license controls standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's rights after partial transfers or limited grants
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who has granted an exclusive right to use and to license others for a particular purpose (or territory) may still have a right to sue for infringements; the scope depends on the terms of the transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Still v. Reading (patentee reserved right to sue despite a five-year grant); other cases show that scope (use, make, sell) and reservations determine who may sue. If transfer only covers an undivided interest, joint suits or joinder rules apply (see related entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may sue for infringements during his ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who has transferred the patent may still maintain an action for infringements committed during his period of ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise notes that where the patentee owned the patent at the time the infringement occurred, he can recover for those infringements even after transferring the patent, but not for infringements that occurred while others owned it (see Moore v. Marsh, Marsh J.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers of undivided interests require joinder
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a transfer covers only an undivided interest in the patent, the transferor must join with the transferee in suits arising out of subsequent infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The action for infringements committed subsequent to the assignment should be brought in the joint names as representing the entire interest; conditional assignments and interests affecting assignor may require equity to secure rights of all parties (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee of entire monopoly must sue in own name (title must be perfected)
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee of the entire interest in the patented invention must sue alone for any infringement committed during his sole ownership; whether assignment was before or after issue is immaterial provided the legal title has been perfected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the title remains imperfect or is only contractual, a court of law cannot take cognizance of an action by the assignee in his own name. Motive for assignment is irrelevant once legal title vests. Cases: Nellis v. Pennock Mfg. Co., Brooks v. Bicknell, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee of undivided or conditional interests cannot sue alone
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee of an undivided interest cannot sue alone but must join co-owners; where assignment is conditional and assignor's interests may be affected, the assignor is a necessary party or equity must be used to protect all parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where interests of assignor are liable to be affected, joinder is required; if joinder impracticable under pleading rules, resort to equity is necessary. An assignee in trust is proper plaintiff until trust fulfilled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grantee of exclusive territorial right must sue alone within territory
rubrics_metrics.description: The grantee of an exclusive territorial interest in the patented invention must sue alone for any infringement committed within his territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early statutes treated grantees differently from assignees, but once the power was conferred the grantee's right to sue is well established. Joint grantees must unite as plaintiffs. Cases: Hobbie v. Smith, Gayler v. Wilder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grantee vs licensee distinction: legal effect controls standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of whether an instrument is a true grant (conveying legal title) or a license (mere permission) controls whether the transferee may sue as owner; short of conveying the entire unqualified monopoly the transferee is a licensee only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To enable purchaser to sue, the assignment must convey the entire and unqualified monopoly in specified territory excluding the patentee as well as others. Cases: Hill v. Whitcomb, Ogle v. Ege, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal representatives must sue for deceased owner's infringements
rubrics_metrics.description: The personal representatives (executor/administrator) of the deceased owner of a patent must be the plaintiffs in an action for infringement committed either during their ownership or that of their decedent; heirs/devisees cannot appear as plaintiffs at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executors/administrators are treated as trustees under Congressional acts and may sue in any federal district without qualifying in local probate courts. If patent issued to one of several executors, that executor alone has legal title to sue. Cases: Woodworth v. Hall, Hodge v. North Missouri R.R. Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments of rights to recover past damages must expressly include right of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments purporting to transfer claims for past infringements must expressly include the right of action; the mere assignment of the patent does not necessarily transfer the right to sue for past infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require express language transferring the right to damages for past infringements. Assignments of such claims are subject to all equities existing between the assignor and alleged infringer; notice to defendant of transfer is necessary to avoid protecting bona fide payments to record plaintiff. Cases: Hamilton v. Rollins, Emerson v. Hubbard, Kaolatype Engraving Co. v. Hoke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee of claims for past infringements may sue but is subject to equities and laches
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee who receives an assignment of claims for past infringements may maintain an action in his own name if the assignment explicitly transfers those claims; such assignee takes subject to all equities (including laches) against the assignor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments of claims pending litigation do not affect the original litigation unless interests require it, but notice to defendant should be given. Laches or other defenses binding on assignor bind assignee. Cases: May v. Logan County of Logan, New York Grape Sugar Co. v. Buffalo Grape Sugar Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must sue in own name according to local law
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper plaintiff must institute the suit in his own name, according to the character imposed upon him by local law; no plaintiff can commence or prosecute a suit in the name of his attorney or other delegate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity rules for married women, infants, corporations, unincorporated associations are governed by state law and charter provisions. Married women may sue separately in some states; unincorporated associations must sue in names of individual members. Cases and examples cited (e.g., Campbell v. James; Goldsmith v. American Paper Collar Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-joinder or misjoinder rules (plaintiffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections for non-joinder or misjoinder of plaintiffs are not favored and must be made in due season or they are waived; a non-joinder may be cured by a disclaimer of title by omitted parties in favor of actual plaintiffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A misjoinder cannot be noticed after final judgment in the Supreme Court; in equity, non-joinder objections are disfavored if parties of record have a legal title. Cases: Graham v. McCormick, Livingston v. Woodworth, Adams v. Howard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary joinder of co-owners/joint patentees
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees having joint ownership or reversionary interests after grantees must be made plaintiffs; same rule applies to joint ownership whether assignees, grantees, or representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of joint owners conveying interest after infringement does not dispense with necessity of joining him as plaintiff. Failure to join necessary persons may require equity. Cases: Moore v. Marsh, Stein v. Goddard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant must be person guilty of act of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who has been guilty of an act of infringement—making, using, selling the patented invention without authority; employing others to do so; accepting and enjoying direct advantage; or acting in complicity—may be made a defendant in an action at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All who perform or unite in performance of an act of infringement may be sued jointly or severally at plaintiff's option, provided they can be served within the court's territorial jurisdiction. The treatise gives detailed modes of wrongful conduct that create liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: All infringers liable; no exemption for infancy/lunacy/coverture; government has separate remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: No exemption from liability exists on grounds of infancy, lunacy, or coverture; the U.S. government when practicing a patented invention without permission may be sued in the Court of Claims for compensation under federal statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although private persons lacking capacity are still liable as defendants, the government is not sued in ordinary courts for patent infringement but has a statutory compensation scheme via the Court of Claims. The treatise contrasts private-party liability with governmental remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of patent does not automatically transfer right to past-claim actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere assignment of the patent does not transfer the right to sue for past infringements unless the assignment expressly includes claims for past damages; courts have held such transfers must be clearly expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several cases hold an assignment by an administrator does not cover past claims; severing past-claim rights from the patent may be impermissible contrary to statutes. Examples: Kaolatype Engraving Co. v. Hoke; Gordon v. Anthony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of transfer of claims pending litigation should be given to defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfers of title and rights of action pendente lite do not affect litigation unless interests require it, but notice of such transfer must be given to the defendant or he will be protected in bona fide payments to the record plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: when an assignor assigns claims during pending litigation, provide notice to the defendant to avoid wrongful payment and defenses arising from lack of notice. Cases: Gear v. Fitch and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal plaintiffs and real parties in interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A nominal plaintiff who contributes funds to pursue litigation may be held to have rights to take such action to protect his own interest, but a nominal plaintiff cannot discontinue a suit brought to protect his licensee; real parties in interest may be permitted to make rights apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text discusses situations where contributors or nominal plaintiffs engage in 'test cases' and the courts' treatment of their rights, including their ability to claim indemnity for costs and limits on their ability to continue suits for others' benefit. Cases: Millar v. Liggett & Myers, Goodyear v. Bishop, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executor/administrator's capacity and venue rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrator or executor of a patentee may sue in any federal district without qualifying in state probate courts within that district; their relation to the patent is that of trustees under acts of Congress, not dependent upon local probate qualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise cites authorities holding executors/administrators may initiate suits in federal circuit courts across states without letters of administration in each state; also notes when patent is re-issued to an executor that acts as proof of authority to sue. Cases: Smith v. Mercer, Woodworth v. Hall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee before patent issue may sue when assignment requests issuance to assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an assignment was made before the patent was granted, but with a request that the patent issue to the assignee, the assignee may sue in his own name even though the patent actually issued to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise cites Consolidated Electric Light Co. v. McKeesport Electric Light Co. and Consolidated Electric Light Co. v. Edison, showing circumstances in which pre-issue assignments confer standing on assignees to sue.
